title: Run record (V0)
description:
One captured run: one workload, attempted by one agent, against one repository state, judged by one oracle. Transcribed from the table "What a run record must carry" in RFC-2026-09-08, which fixes the shape rather than the field names — the shape being what makes the one query a router would eventually need answerable at all: the same workload, on the same repository state, under the same oracle, across different models.

Every component of that table is required here, because the table's third column is a list of things that cannot be added later. `human_baseline` is the exception, and it is required by constraint rather than by prose — the relationship those constraints enforce is stated on `pairing.baseline`. Its absence is what stops a row from carrying an economic claim.

This record is metadata. Prompts, file content and tool arguments may be customer or private-repository material and do not appear in it: `execution.event_stream` references the stream, it does not carry it (RFC §Constraints 5).

V0 observes and does not route. No field here expresses a routing decision or a model-selection recommendation, and none may be added that does.

`workload.domain`, `workload.scope` and `oracle.id` are left open and narrowed by whatever composes this schema, in the way `verdict.base.schema.json` leaves `agent` and `scope_class` open.

This file carries no `$id`: every reference to it is a relative path, so it resolves from the filesystem — offline, in CI, and in a fresh clone alike.

run_id.description: Identity of this run. Not from the RFC table: a row that cannot be named cannot be de-duplicated, referenced by a fence, or paired.

started_at.description: When the run began, RFC 3339, UTC. Not from the RFC table: a fence is dated, so a row that is not dated is on neither side of it.

workload.description: RFC table: `Workload` — fingerprint, domain, scope, phase, complexity. `fingerprint` identifies the task, under a stability qualification stated on the field itself; the key that joins one preregistered comparison is `pairing.group_id`. They are deliberately different keys.

fingerprint.description:
An opaque identity for the task. Under `reg:` it is stable over time: the same value when the same task is run again after a fence, under a new oracle or a new model snapshot, so that "the same task under different conditions" is something the dataset can say. The stability holds under both derivations: neither carries a key, so nothing rotates and nothing hands the same task a second identity.

It is not the join key for a preregistered comparison — `pairing.group_id` is. This is a stated departure from the RFC table, whose third column calls the fingerprint "the join key for paired runs": `pairing`, itself not from the table, took that role, because a key that is declared beats a key that is recovered, and grouping rows by fingerprint to reconstruct a comparison is the post-hoc operation `pairing` exists to prevent.

Never a bare digest of the task's text. A plain hash of a short description is a confirmation oracle: anyone who guesses the sentence verifies it against a published row, which would reopen through this field exactly the leak `scope` is closed to prevent, in a form that looks safe because it looks like a hash.

Two sanctioned derivations, one per producer class, and the prefix says which — because two producers deriving one task differently is the way "stable across arms" fails that no validator can see.

`reg:<id>` — an opaque identifier assigned by the private task registry when the task is planned, and the first choice. Preregistration already requires the task's description to exist in a private place before any arm runs; that document is a registry, and a registry assigns identifiers. Nothing is derived, so nothing can be reversed and no input of the task's can be guessed at all. That is why it is the first choice rather than a preference.

`ci:<digest>` — a plain SHA-256 over `(repository, pull request number, head sha)`, for a producer with no access to the registry: the CI bot. IT CARRIES NO KEY, and the paragraph above says why one is not needed rather than being excepted: a confirmation oracle matters where the guessed input is not otherwise in the row, and these three are. `repository_state` REQUIRES the repository and the commit in clear in the same row, so a MAC would be guarding what is printed beside it — in either inbox, since whoever reads the row reads `repository_state` too — while its rotation would hand every task a new identity and write a fence, losing the stability `reg:` is preferred for. The argument rests on `repository_state.repository` staying required: if that goes, the key comes back. ADR-087, amendment of 2026-09-17.

The two prefixes name disjoint universes of task — planned tasks, and CI events — so a value from one never joins a value from the other, and never does so silently.

A fingerprint derived from anything model-specific silently unpairs the runs it exists to pair.

domain.description:
The workload's domain. Left open and narrowed by the composing schema. V0's first domain is documentation and the agent layer, and it is an instrumentation and calibration workload, not a representative one.

Two workloads whose oracle judges different things are two domains however alike they look. A sweep is judged on output the agent produced; a review is judged on a pull request the agent did not write. Averaging their outcomes under one domain name produces exactly the scientific-looking and meaningless figure this record exists to prevent, so the distinction is made here, from the first row, and not recovered later.

scope.description:
What kind of workload this was, as a term from the domain's vocabulary — `adr-amendment`, `frontmatter-backfill`, `spi-javadoc`. Left open here and narrowed to an enum by the composing schema, exactly as `verdict.base.schema.json` leaves `scope_class` open.

Deliberately not prose. Free text here would be the one field in the record carrying semantics, and `Add slab-pool eviction under io_uring` or `prepare pricing for design partner X` is a roadmap in a single row — a leak that does not depend on the source repository being private, because a public repository can carry a workload that is not. What the run did is held by `fingerprint`, which is opaque; what kind of thing it was is held here, from a closed list. A vocabulary is also the only form of this field that can be grouped on, which prose never could.

phase.description: Which phase of the workload this run covers, where a planner decomposed it. Absent until V2 produces phase-level outcomes; rows that carry it and rows that do not are never averaged together.

complexity.description:
The annotation, deliberately three-valued. RFC §Risks records that a single-rater, unanchored 1–10 scale is mostly noise and is the step skipped in week three, and that `too-weak | appropriate | overkill` is cheap and carries most of the signal. It judges the model that ran against this workload, it is an annotation, and it is never an input to anything V0 emits.

`rater` and `rated_at` are required with it, and neither is decoration. V1's exit criterion is "annotation noise quantified", which is computable only as agreement between raters, so a row that does not say who judged it leaves a second rater nothing to be compared against. `rated_at` is the other axis: its distance from `started_at` is the only evidence that a judgement was made on the run rather than from a memory of it.

rater.description: Who made the judgement. Required from the first row because inter-rater agreement is not reconstructible later, and because the dataset, the oracle and the annotation currently share one author, which is exactly SCB §0.3's warning.

rated_at.description: When the judgement was made, RFC 3339, UTC.

pairing.description:
Not from the RFC table. Paired runs are the RFC's primary collection mode — the same task across N models, at far smaller n than observational rows across heterogeneous tasks would need — and this component exists so the group is declared before the arms run rather than recovered afterwards by grouping on `workload.fingerprint` and `repository_state`. That difference is the preregistration discipline itself: a group assigned in advance is an artefact of the design; a group recovered by a query is a query, and a query can be re-run until it says something.

A pointer to a counterpart run was considered and rejected. The first arm written cannot know the run_id of an arm that does not exist yet, so it would have to be rewritten, which `inbox/` forbids; and at three arms a one-sided pointer becomes a clique to maintain.

Absent on an unpaired observational row.

group_id.description: Assigned before any arm runs. Every arm of one group carries the same value, and no arm assigns it.

arm.description:
Which slot of the plan this row fills. Unique within `group_id`: a repeated condition is separate slots — `frontier-1`, `frontier-2`, `frontier-3` — never one label on three rows. That is what lets `arms_planned` stay a count of expected rows, so an incomplete group is still detected when the missing rows are replicates of one condition. SCB's own design, 3 runs × 3 arms, is nine slots here, not three.

It labels the slot, not the model — `agent` already names that — and variance within one condition is recovered by grouping the group's rows on `agent`, which is what `agent` is for. A second field for replicate count would only mean something in terms of this one, so there is not one.

This is a rule across files, which this schema cannot express; the inbox validator owns it — see `inbox/README.md`, `## Rules a schema cannot see`.

arms_planned.description:
How many rows the group was planned to contain, so an incomplete group is detectable without inferring what was intended. It counts the model arms: a human arm produces `human_baseline` on every row of the group and is not itself a row.

What makes this count exact is stated on `arm`.

baseline.description: Declared when the group is planned, not discovered when it finishes. `human`: a human arm ran, and every row of the group carries `human_baseline` — enforced by a constraint below. `none`: no human reference exists, which is legitimate and is the case for the cheapest groups this layer has (a CI runner matrix is a paired run without a human arm), and which means the group can never carry an economic claim, for the reason stated on `human_baseline`; this field is that reason in a form V1 can read without re-deciding it row by row.

agent.description: RFC table: `Agent` / `Model` / `Harness` — provider, model id, snapshot, client + version, system-prompt hash. All required: a row without them is uninterpretable once a snapshot moves. SCB §8 defines a model reference as id + snapshot + harness + system-prompt hash, and this component is that reference with one substitution it states rather than hides — `system_prompt_sha256` covers the instructions the repository controls, and `harness.client` with `harness.version` stands in for the client's own system prompt, which a producer under a hosted action cannot read. The substitution is a weakening, not an equivalence, and the hole it leaves is stated on `system_prompt_sha256`. That is why the harness is part of the reference, and why a harness change writes a new `instrument.fence`.

model_id.description: The vendor's identifier for the model, as the vendor writes it. The pattern is deliberately wide — vendors write `/`, `@` and `:` into these (`meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B`, `llama3:70b`) and this field does not get to legislate someone else's naming. It is here at all so that `model_snapshot` can state the SAME body: the marked form is `unresolved:` followed by this value, and a snapshot field that admitted fewer characters than the id it marks would make some ids impossible to mark. Any change here changes that one too.

model_snapshot.description:
The dated or versioned snapshot behind `model_id`. An id whose snapshot moved names a different model, and rows either side of the move are not comparable.

Where the runtime exposes no snapshot for the model that took the turns, the field carries `unresolved:<model_id>` — the alias, marked so that neither a reader nor a query can read it as a snapshot. An unexposed snapshot is a property of the INSTRUMENT, not a value of the datum: `instrument.fence` carries the state, rows are comparable within a fence and never across one. The bare alias is refused, because one alias may name different weights at different times and a row that cannot tell is worse than a row that says it cannot. `model_snapshot` equal to `model_id` is that refusal, and it is enforced by `tools/inbox_validate.py` — JSON Schema compares a value against a constant, never against its sibling. So is the other half: what follows `unresolved:` must be THIS row's `model_id`, because a mark naming some other alias marks nothing.

The pattern is `unresolved:` over `model_id`'s own body, and the two are written to stay that way — a snapshot field narrower than the id it marks would leave vendor ids containing `/` or `@` with no valid marked form at all.

The SAME PARITY IN LENGTH, which is the half that was missed the first time: this field's `maxLength` is `model_id`'s plus the eleven characters of `unresolved:`. Equal caps would have left every id of 118 characters or more unmarkable — the identical defect, one axis over, under a commit claiming the defect closed. ADR-086, amendment of 2026-09-17.

harness.description: The client that ran the model, and its version. One model under two clients is two harnesses, not one.

system_prompt_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the instructions the repository controls: the prompt text in the workflow, the routine file it points at, and the agent files in force at `repository_state.commit`, canonicalised by a method the producer documents. It is deliberately not a hash of the client's own system prompt — under a hosted action that text is not available to the producer at all, and a change to it is proxied, imperfectly, by `harness.version` — a client that changes its system prompt without changing its version is invisible here, which is a stated hole in the model reference rather than a covered case. A change to the canonicalisation is a change to the instrument and writes a new `instrument.fence`. Left undefined, this field fills with whatever was convenient, and a fence then fails to fire on the change that mattered.

repository_state.description: RFC table: `RepositoryState` — commit, bundle version, dirty flag. "The same repository state" is otherwise unverifiable. It is not a join key: the arms of one comparison share a repository state by definition, so within a `group_id` this is an invariant rather than a key, and the key is `pairing.group_id`. This is a rule across files, which this schema cannot express; the inbox validator owns it — see `inbox/README.md`, `## Rules a schema cannot see`.

repository.description: Which repository the commit is in. Not from the RFC table: a commit sha alone cannot be resolved across twenty sibling repositories.

visibility.description:
Not from the RFC table. The repository's visibility in ADR-020's taxonomy, which has exactly these two values; `public-staged` is deprecated and never appears here. Recorded at capture time rather than resolved later: a repository can be opened afterwards, and a row is subject to the visibility in force when it was written.

The producer maps the host's own answer onto this vocabulary fail-closed. `gh repo view --json visibility` returns `PUBLIC | PRIVATE | INTERNAL`; only `PUBLIC` becomes `public`, and everything else — including a visibility the producer could not establish — becomes `enterprise-private`.

The rule runs one way only. A repository can also leave public — archived, or moved behind an ADR-020 mirror — and a row already published does not come back. Nothing here is repaired by correcting a visibility afterwards.

bundle_version.description: The pinned `exeris-agents` bundle version in the checkout. The bundle carries the rules the run was subject to, so a bundle change is a change to the run's conditions.

dirty.description: Whether the working tree carried uncommitted changes. Required, and `false` is a claim: without it, `commit` is an assertion about a tree nobody checked.

execution.description: RFC table: `Execution` — event stream, tool calls, turns, wall time, with metadata separated from potentially sensitive content. That separation is this component's shape: the counts are here, the stream is referenced. Prompts, file content and tool arguments never appear in a run record.

wall_time_ms.description: Wall time is one of the two units that survive a comparison across models — see `accounting.usage`.

event_stream.description:
A reference to the run's event record, never the record itself. Under a local runtime that is the dispatcher's normalised stream. In CI, where no sink is wired, it is whatever execution log the runner emits — whether such a log exists in a usable shape has not been verified on a real run and is an open question, not an assumption this schema makes.

Whatever it points at may contain prompts, file content and tool arguments, so the artefact is stored outside `inbox/` and never beside the row. `sha256` keeps the reference verifiable after a retention window has taken the artefact away, and `event_count` keeps the row summarisable once it is gone.

accounting.description:
RFC table: `Accounting` — mode, usage, provider-reported cost. Under a subscription there is no per-run price, and mixing modes in one column corrupts every later cost conclusion, undetectably. The `allOf` below is that sentence made enforceable: only an `api` row may carry a cost.

A runner's own tooling may report a USD figure under a subscription by applying a price list to the token counts. That figure is imputed, not reported, and the constraint below rejects it — but the producer is expected to drop it deliberately, not to have simply failed to look for it.

mode.description: `api`: a per-run price exists and the provider reported it. `subscription`: no per-run price exists, and none may be imputed. `local`: the cost is hardware and wall time, and is not a provider figure.

usage.description: Token counts. Comparable only within one model (SCB §7.1); across models the units are USD and wall time.

provider_reported_cost.description: What the provider billed for this run, as the provider reported it — never a figure this layer computed from a price list.

allOf.$comment: Under a subscription or a local model there is no per-run price. A cost on such a row is imputed, and an imputed cost is indistinguishable from a reported one once it is in the column.

oracle.description: RFC table: `Oracle` — id, version, and calibration state. Without the calibration state, an average across six months of drifting oracles looks scientific and means nothing. `calibration` is required for that reason, not as a nicety.

id.description:
Which oracle judged this run. Left open and narrowed by the composing schema: V0's is the documentation and agent-layer guardrail suite, whose scope is structural consistency and never whether the work is any good. The System Construction Benchmark becomes a second implementation behind the same interface at its Phase 4, carrying its own calibration state.

One oracle id used across two domains names two different oracles and must never be summarised as one. Which oracle judges a review run is settled by ADR-086 §D — two review domains of different standing, not one — and `workload.domain` carries why they must be two.

calibration.description: The oracle's own mutation-suite result at the time of this run — for example suite `docs-mutation-v1`, status `pass`, result `8/8`. `status` is three-valued like `checks_run` in `verdict.base.schema.json`: a suite that has not been run is `not-run`, and `not-run` is not a pass.

result.description: The suite's score as it was published, e.g. `8/8`.

outcome.description: RFC table: `Outcome` — fail-closed. A run whose gates did not run is `UNKNOWN`, never a pass. `FALSE_DONE` is the run that claimed completion the oracle contradicts; `UNREACHABLE` is the run that never got far enough to be judged.

instrument.description: RFC table: `InstrumentVersion` / `Fence` — capture version, and the dated fence in force. Rows either side of a fence are never summarised in one figure, so a row that does not name its fence cannot be summarised at all.

fence.description: The dated fence in force when this row was written. A change to the oracle, the harness, the dispatcher or a model snapshot writes a new one; what may happen to a row a fence marks is owned by `inbox/README.md`.

human_baseline.description:
RFC table: `HumanBaseline` — on paired tasks: human time, outcome, changes. A V0 requirement, not a follow-up: `Haiku: $0.10, 95% TRUE_DONE` reads as a triumph until one learns a human does the same work in seven minutes and Haiku takes forty-two, at which point the economic interpretation inverts. A cost figure with no human reference point is not interpretable, only quotable.

It is duplicated onto every row of its group — `pairing.baseline` owns that relationship — and duplication has one failure mode: divergence. Two rows of one group carrying different human baselines are not one row being wrong — they are a group that cannot be interpreted. Every `human_baseline` within a `group_id` must therefore be byte-for-byte identical — a rule across files, and one that makes the human-arm-first protocol observable as a side effect: a row written before the baseline existed cannot be identical to the rows written after it. This is a rule across files, which this schema cannot express; the inbox validator owns it — see `inbox/README.md`, `## Rules a schema cannot see`.

The trigger for outgrowing this shape, named here so it is recognised rather than discovered: the moment this object needs a second field about the *human* rather than about the *work*, it stops being a field and becomes a record that rows reference. `who` is the first such field, so the trigger is close.

outcome.description: Judged by the same oracle at the same calibration state, or the baseline is not a baseline.

allOf.$comment: A group planned with a human arm carries the baseline on every one of its rows. This is writable at capture time only because the human arm runs first — a protocol condition stated in README.md, which also keeps the human from having seen a model's output. The constraint assumes that protocol; it cannot enforce it.

A group planned without a human arm cannot acquire one afterwards. A baseline attached to a `none` group is a post-hoc addition to a preregistered design, which is what `pairing` exists to prevent; the correct record of a human attempt made later is a new group declared with `baseline: human`.

fail_closed_uncalibrated_oracle.$comment: Fail-closed, from RFC-2026-09-08 §Testing: until the oracle's mutation suite passes as a suite, V0 records outcomes as UNKNOWN. An oracle whose PASS has never been contradicted by a known-broken input is unvalidated, so neither its TRUE_DONE nor its FALSE_DONE is admissible as a label.
